newsitem.title: GERMANY: Miners keep vigil in Bonn, protest at subsidy cuts.
newsitem.headline: Miners keep vigil in Bonn, protest at subsidy cuts.

text.p: Thousands of German coal miners camped in Bonn's government quarter and vowed to keep up protests at subsidy cuts on Wednesday despite a union call to wait for the outcome of talks on Thursday with the government.

About 3,000 angry pitworkers rode into Bonn in buses headed by a convoy of about 100 motorcycles late on Tuesday to keep up pressure on the government to drop plans to cut subsidies that they say will put more half of them out of work.
A few kept vigil outside the headquarters of the pro-market Free Democrats (FDP) -- the driving force behind the cuts and chief target of their wrath.
Wrapped in blankets, they huddled together and burnt fires in braziers to keep warm.

"We're staying here until Thursday when a decision has to be made. We're only going home when we have a clear answer from the government on how much money we're going to get," said miner Ruediger Heinze, 36, from the town of Dinslaken.
"And we're not planning to go home empty-handed," he said.

about 13,000 angry pitworkers earlier laid siege to Bonn's government quarter and blockaded a major highway on Tuesday, when union leaders were scheduled to meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl for crisis talks.

But when Kohl postponed the meeting to Thursday, saying he would not meet them in an atmosphere of intimidation, hundreds forced their way through a police barricade and scuffles broke out with police.
Calm was restored, but the mood remained tense.
At a rally on Tuesday, union leaders and their political mentors the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) urged the miners to go home but be ready to return en masse if did not meet Kohl.

While most headed back home to Germany's ailing steel and coal industrial Ruhr heartland and the state of Saar on the French border, a hard core stayed on and 3,000 miners who had held demonstrations earlier during the day in Saar joined them.
The confrontation with the miners is perhaps the most dramatic sign yet of growing discontent with welfare cuts, budget savings and job losses.
Miners in Germany's 18 pits downed their tools on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) by 2005 instead of a promised 6.5 billion.

The Berliner Zeitung daily, citing government sources, reported that the government was now prepared to give some ground to the miners by offering an additional 300 million marks a year in payments until 2000.
Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told ZDF television that the government was standing by its plans to cut coal subsidies to 3.8 billion marks from nine billion until 2005.
He added, however, that he saw the possibility that an agreement with union leaders could be reached.
Wolfgang Gerhardt leader of the FDP, Kohl's junior coalition partner, told German radio government officials might be prepared to be more flexible on the timetable for phasing out the subsidies.
Currently Bonn pays over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
Mining union IG Bergbau says the government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt of the FDP said there was scant room to compromise when each mining job cost the government 130,000 marks ($76,200) a year.

"Our offer means we are providing more than 50 billion marks for the mining sector over nine years," he told German Radio. "Coal subsidies have been declining for many decades, and it was well known that there would be a cut in 1997 of the order that has been proposed."
